conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported, citing landmark trial evidence (MAP.3) and official cancer organization summaries showing a 65% reduction in invasive breast cancer incidence among postmenopausal women at elevated risk.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported, not false. The key evidence is the MAP.3 randomized prevention trial, reported in *NEJM*: exemestane significantly reduced invasive breast-cancer incidence among postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk. The reported reduction was 65% over a median three-year follow-up (0.19% annual incidence with exemestane versus 0.55% with placebo).  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507

NCI’s current prevention summary independently states that, in high-risk postmenopausal women, three years of exemestane reduced breast-cancer incidence by 65% compared with controls.  
https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/hp/breast-prevention-pdq

**Why someone might still question the claim:** the evidence addresses incidence over relatively short follow-up, not a demonstrated reduction in breast-cancer mortality or a guarantee of benefit for every postmenopausal woman. It applies to women at elevated/moderately increased risk, not average-risk women. Prevention treatment also requires balancing benefit against adverse effects: the USPSTF describes aromatase inhibitors as having “small to moderate harms,” while finding that net benefit is greater as baseline breast-cancer risk rises.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction
